content.overview: BNS s. 31 — Communication made in good faith.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Communication made in good faith. BNS restatement of IPC 93. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 93. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 31 is the rule on “Communication made in good faith”. The section provides that no communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 31 exists so that “Communication made in good faith” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
31. No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person

Essential ingredients
1. No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, a surgeon, in good faith, communicates to a patient his opinion that he cannot live. The patient dies in consequence of the shock. A has committed no offence, though he knew it to be likely that the communication might cause the patient’s death

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 31 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 31 (Communication made in good faith) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 31 (Communication made in good faith), Chapter III — General Exceptions.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 31 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 31 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.
